screens.title: Symptoms and root causes of corruption
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystem corruption shows itself in a handful of consistent ways. Typical symptoms include Input/output error messages when reading or writing files, directories that become inaccessible, files that appear to vanish, and unusually slow file operations. These symptoms arise from either metadata damage, which affects directory structures and inodes, or data corruption where file contents are unreadable. Common causes map predictably to these symptoms: sudden power loss or incomplete writes can leave metadata inconsistent; hardware faults like bad sectors cause input and output errors and unreadable files; improper unmounts or kernel panics can leave a filesystem marked dirty; and filesystem-specific bugs or driver issues can corrupt metadata. Modern journaling filesystems mitigate some risks because they record pending metadata operations in a journal, enabling recovery of structural consistency after a crash, but they do not protect file contents from underlying disk errors. A common misconception is that running fsck will always restore lost files; fsck repairs structural consistency and may discard irrecoverably corrupted data. The practical test is to reproduce symptoms on a disposable VM, capture dmesg and syslog messages, and then correlate input and output errors with failing S. M. A. R. T. attributes to decide whether to repair or replace hardware. When you see these signs, prioritize a read-only snapshot or image, then proceed with diagnosis to avoid further damage. How confident are you at distinguishing metadata failure from raw device failure?

keyIdea.text: Match observable errors to likely causes before attempting repairs — that guides safe next steps.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Symptoms & Causes
Definition

Filesystem corruption is damage to metadata or data structures that prevents normal access or causes data loss.

Common symptoms
  • Input/output errors from read or write syscalls
  • Missing files or inaccessible directories
  • Slow or stalled file operations
  • Filesystem marked dirty at boot
Causes
  • Sudden power loss or incomplete writes
  • Hardware faults like bad sectors
  • Incorrect unmounts or kernel panics
  • Metadata corruption from bugs or driver issues
Key Takeaway

Observe logs and S.M.A.R.T. data before repair; preserve a read-only image when possible to avoid losing recoverable data.

Example scenario

A server shows repeated 'Input/output error' lines in syslog and files disappear after an abrupt power event. dmesg reports I/O errors on /dev/sdb. Correlating these symptoms with SMART reallocated sector counts confirms that the disk is failing.

What not to do

Do not run write-heavy repairs or mount the device to force reads; this can make recovery harder.

Check your understanding
  • Which logs or commands help you decide if a disk is failing?
  • When is a journal insufficient to protect data?

screens.title: Safe use of fsck and filesystem-specific tools
screens.narratorSegment: The fsck family is the primary utility for checking and repairing Linux filesystems. The most important safety rule is simple: only run fsck on an unmounted filesystem. Running fsck on a mounted or in-use filesystem risks further corruption because the on-disk state can change concurrently. For non-root partitions unmount them first with the umount command. For root or busy systems boot a rescue environment or single-user mode so the root filesystem can be unmounted or mounted read-only. Fsck is a front-end that dispatches to filesystem-specific checkers like fsck. ext4 or xfs_repair for XFS. Important flags change behavior: -y automatically answers yes to repair prompts, useful in controlled labs but risky in production because it accepts destructive fixes; -f forces a check even if the filesystem appears clean. For XFS, use xfs_repair and prefer a dry run with -n to preview changes without writing. A common misconception is that -y is always safe; in fact it can permit large deletions without inspection. Before running repairs, capture a disk image or snapshot if the data is valuable. After repairs, check filesystem integrity by mounting read-only and verifying key files. This process reduces guesswork and prevents accidental data loss by enforcing a disciplined, recoverable workflow.

keyIdea.text: Unmount first, prefer dry-run for unknown cases, and avoid -y on production systems unless you have a tested recovery plan.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Safe fsck Usage
One-sentence rule

Do not run fsck on a mounted filesystem; use a rescue environment for root repairs.

Common fsck flags
  • -y: automatically apply fixes (use with caution)
  • -f: force check even if clean
  • -c: run badblocks integration (Ext filesystems)
XFS special case

Use xfs_repair and prefer the -n dry run to preview required repairs before committing them.

Key Takeaway

Preserve a copy before repairs. Use dry-run and avoid blind "yes" in production.

Step-by-step checklist
  1. Gather logs: dmesg, syslog, and /var/log/messages for I/O symptoms.
  2. Confirm device name with lsblk or blkid to avoid wrong partition mistakes.
  3. Unmount the filesystem: sudo umount /dev/sdXN.
  4. Run fsck with appropriate flags; prefer dry-run options when available.
  5. Mount read-only to confirm recovery, then mount read-write after verification.
Misconception

Running fsck while mounted is safe if it's read-only — false. Even reads can race with system activity; unmount or use rescue mode.

screens.title: Running fsck on root: rescue workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When the root filesystem itself is corrupted, the only safe path is to isolate it from normal operations before making repairs. The typical workflow is: boot into a rescue image or live USB, or use single-user mode where possible. In a rescue environment the root filesystem is not mounted as the system root, so you can run fsck safely on the device. Begin by identifying the correct device name using lsblk and blkid to avoid operating on the wrong partition. Capture a disk image snapshot if the data is important. Then run fsck with the appropriate options; for an Ext4 root partition you might use fsck -fcc to include a bad block scan. If you must force checks, use -f judiciously. After fsck completes, mount the partition read-only and inspect critical files like /etc/fstab and boot files before rebooting. A misconception is that rebooting immediately after fsck always fixes boot issues; sometimes filesystem metadata was repaired but bootloader or kernel image files are damaged and need separate restoration. The rescue workflow both secures the data and gives you time to confirm the system boots cleanly before returning to production.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Rescue Workflow
Terminal checklist
# Inspect devices
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT
sudo blkid /dev/sda1

# If root is corrupted: boot a live CD/USB, then
sudo fsck -fcc /dev/sda1

# Mount read-only to inspect
sudo mount -o ro /dev/sda1 /mnt/rescue
ls /mnt/rescue/etc /mnt/rescue/boot
The code above shows the safe sequence: identify, image, fsck with badblock scan, then mount read-only to check important files.
Supporting notes
  • Always confirm device names; mistakes here can destroy other partitions.
  • Use a read-only mount to verify configuration and boot files before making changes.
  • When in doubt, make a dd image of the partition for offline analysis.
Common mistake

Booting normally and running fsck from a mounted root risks overwriting live metadata and losing changes you need.

screens.title: Diagnosing LVM issues
screens.narratorSegment: LVM adds a flexible layer between filesystems and physical disks but also adds diagnostic complexity. When a logical volume becomes inaccessible, you must examine Physical Volumes (PVs), Volume Groups (VGs), and Logical Volumes (LVs) to find where the fault lies. Start with sudo pvdisplay to list physical devices and their status, then vgdisplay to inspect the volume group and see which PVs are missing or failed, and finally lvdisplay to check the logical volumes. A typical failure path is a PV that went offline due to a bad disk or controller issue. If a PV is missing, the VG may show reduced capacity and LVs may be inactive. In software RAID setups the underlying PVs might themselves be RAID devices; check /proc/mdstat and mdadm --detail /dev/mdX to map those relationships. Replace a failed physical disk in RAID first, then allow mdadm and the RAID to rebuild before attempting LVM repairs. A frequent misconception is to try to repair LVM metadata before ensuring the underlying disks are healthy; doing so can corrupt higher-level structures. Always resolve hardware-level faults first, then rescan PVs and restore VG/LV state. The goal is to preserve logical volume metadata while restoring the missing physical pieces beneath it.

keyIdea.text: Diagnose from PV → VG → LV and fix or replace failing physical devices before modifying LVM metadata.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › LVM Diagnosis
Component mapping
Physical Volume (PV)

A disk or partition reported to LVM. Use pvdisplay to check status and UUIDs.

Volume Group (VG)

Aggregation of PVs. vgdisplay shows free space and missing PVs.

Logical Volume (LV)

Block device used by filesystems. lvdisplay reveals LV status and attributes.

Commands to inspect:

sudo pvdisplay
sudo vgdisplay
sudo lvdisplay
sudo pvs -o +devices
Example

If vgdisplay shows a missing PV after a disk failure, first repair or replace the disk and rebuild RAID if used, then run pvscan and vgchange -ay to reactivate the VG.

Pro tip

Map LVM devices to /dev entries before making changes and keep a copy of vg metadata via vgcfgbackup.

screens.title: RAID behaviors and recovery patterns
screens.narratorSegment: RAID provides redundancy but recovery steps depend on the RAID level and the nature of the failure. Software RAID1 and RAID5 tolerate a single disk failure (RAID1 mirrors, RAID5 stripes with parity); however, if failures exceed the array's tolerance or if metadata is corrupted, the array can degrade or fail. Start diagnosis with cat /proc/mdstat to see array state and use mdadm --detail /dev/mdX for member status. If a disk fails in RAID1 or RAID5, you can replace it and run mdadm --add to start rebuilding. Rebuilds read data from remaining members and reconstruct lost content using parity; they should be monitored closely because a second failure during rebuild can be catastrophic. Controller or metadata issues may require assembling the array manually with mdadm --assemble --force, but forcing assembly is risky and should be done only when you have a recent backup or a forensic image. A common mistake is adding a disk with an unexpected partition table; ensure new drives are prepared correctly before adding them. Monitoring arrays regularly and testing rebuilds in a lab helps you practice the exact sequence. The practical rule is: repair the lowest level first (replace physical drives), then rebuild RAID, then restore LVM or filesystem layers above it.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › RAID Recovery
RAID status commands
cat /proc/mdstat
sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md0
sudo mdadm --add /dev/md0 /dev/sdb
sudo mdadm --manage /dev/md0 --remove /dev/sdX
Use --detail to see which member is faulty and the rebuild percent. Always prefer safe add/remove sequences rather than forcing operations when possible.
Rebuild example

If /proc/mdstat shows one device missing in a RAID5 array, replace the failed disk, prepare partitions, then run mdadm --add. Monitor the rebuild until clean.

Gotcha

Do not interrupt a rebuild unless you have a tested recovery plan. Interruptions can leave the array inconsistent.

screens.title: Bad blocks and when to retire a drive
screens.narratorSegment: Bad blocks are physical defects on a storage device that make data unreadable or unwritable from those sectors. Drives often remap bad sectors internally using spare blocks, which is transparent until remapped counts climb. A small isolated bad block may be harmless once marked, but a growing number indicates imminent failure. Use badblocks to perform a scan and detect problematic sectors. For Ext-family filesystems e2fsck -c (or fsck -c) integrates badblocks results and writes those blocks into the filesystem's bad block inode so the OS will avoid allocating them. Importantly, badblocks can be run in read-only or non-destructive modes; destructive writes will overwrite data, so always use a non-destructive scan when scanning an active filesystem. If badblocks reports many errors, the correct action is to replace the drive rather than attempt elaborate repairs. A misconception is that marking bad blocks makes a failing drive healthy; marking avoids immediate allocation but does not stop the hardware from developing further defects. The practical approach is to combine badblock scans with SMART monitoring; rising reallocated or pending sector counts plus badblocks failures should trigger replacement and restore from backups.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Bad Blocks
What are bad blocks?

Physical sectors on a drive that cannot reliably store or return data. Drives can remap, but increasing counts indicate failure.

Tool

badblocks scans a device; for Ext filesystems, use e2fsck -c to integrate results safely into filesystem metadata.

Example command
# Non-destructive read-only scan
sudo badblocks -sv /dev/sdb

# Integrate with Ext filesystem via e2fsck
sudo e2fsck -c /dev/sdb1
If badblocks finds many sectors, schedule drive replacement and restore from backups instead of relying on marking alone.

screens.title: Integrating badblocks with fsck
screens.narratorSegment: When you suspect physical sector issues, combine badblocks and fsck to both detect and record bad sectors so the filesystem avoids them. Start with a non-destructive badblocks scan: badblocks -sv /dev/sdX shows progress and reports sector addresses. For an Ext-family filesystem, use e2fsck -c to run badblocks and then add the detected blocks to the filesystem's bad block inode. The combined command sequence safely marks bad sectors without overwriting user data. After running e2fsck -c, check the count of marked bad blocks and cross-reference with SMART attributes such as Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector to decide whether to keep or replace the drive. A common misconception is that e2fsck -c fixes all problems; marking blocks only prevents allocation to those sectors, but it cannot recover data already lost to hardware defects. After marking, monitor the drive closely and plan a replacement if new bad blocks appear. In production, perform this work during maintenance windows and always have backups. The practical confirmation step is to remount and verify files, and to rerun smartctl to check whether pending sector counts changed after the mark.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Badblocks + fsck
Recommended command flow

sudo badblocks -sv /dev/sdb

# Run e2fsck which invokes badblocks and marks bad blocks in FS
sudo e2fsck -c /dev/sdb1
Use read-only or non-destructive scans whenever you need to preserve data. Only run destructive tests on disposable media.
Interpretation checklist
  • Compare badblocks output with S.M.A.R.T. pending/reallocated counts.
  • If many blocks are marked, schedule an immediate replacement.
  • After marking, remount and verify important files are readable.

Marking is temporary mitigation. Persistent or expanding bad block counts require drive replacement and restore from backup.

screens.title: Terminal lab: simulate corruption and repair with fsck
screens.narratorSegment: This terminal-focused lab walks you through creating a disposable 2GB virtual disk, formatting it as Ext4, simulating corruption with dd, then repairing it with fsck. Use a VM snapshot or isolated environment — never run these steps on production disks. First create a partition and format: use fdisk to make /dev/sdb1 and mkfs. ext4 to format. Mount it, write a few test files, then unmount. To simulate corruption, dd can overwrite a specific block range with random data; this is destructive, so triple-check the device path. After simulating corruption, run sudo fsck -y /dev/sdb1 in the rescue environment to let fsck attempt repairs. When fsck finishes, mount read-only and inspect files to determine salvageability. The -y flag automates acceptance of repairs; understand that it may discard data without prompting, so in real incidents prefer interactive checks or backups. As a verification step, interpret fsck output: look for messages about inode or directory fixes and any files moved to lost+found. A common misconception is that fsck -y always restores files exactly — instead it restores structural consistency and may place orphaned files in lost+found. After the lab, practice restoring from a backup to confirm you can recover lost content when needed.

keyIdea.title: Lab purpose
keyIdea.text: Use an isolated VM to safely practice corruption and fsck repairs; interpret fsck output to confirm recovery and limits.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Terminal steps (do in a VM)
# Create partition and format
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb   # n p 1 w
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

# Mount and add data
sudo mkdir /mnt/testfs
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/testfs
sudo touch /mnt/testfs/file{1..5}.txt
echo "Some data" | sudo tee /mnt/testfs/data.txt
sudo umount /mnt/testfs

# Simulate corruption (DANGER: ensure /dev/sdb1 is correct)
sudo dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/sdb1 bs=1M count=1 seek=10 status=progress

# Repair
sudo fsck -y /dev/sdb1

# Verify
sudo mount -o ro /dev/sdb1 /mnt/testfs
ls /mnt/testfs
cat /mnt/testfs/data.txt || echo "data unreadable"
sudo umount /mnt/testfs
The lab forces you to interpret fsck messages: files reported as orphaned will appear in lost+found, and I/O errors during mounting indicate unrecoverable data. Practice restoring from backups after the lab to complete the recovery workflow.

screens.title: Monitoring & prevention strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Prevention reduces incidents. Set up S. M. A. R. T. monitoring using smartctl to collect attributes like Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector that often precede failures. Schedule regular checks and alerts with smartd or monitoring tools to notify you before errors become critical. Complement SMART with periodic filesystem checks on non-production partitions or during maintenance windows to catch metadata issues early. For RAID and LVM, monitor mdstat and LVM metadata health, and test rebuilds in a lab to be familiar with timelines and failure modes. The most important prevention is a robust backup strategy that includes frequent backups and occasional restore tests. Backups allow you to replace drives without fearing data loss and enable more aggressive repair choices in emergency situations. A common misconception is that RAID replaces the need for backups; RAID protects against hardware failure during operation but does not protect against user error, filesystem corruption, or catastrophic multi-disk failure. Design your monitoring and backup plan with time-to-recovery and RPO objectives in mind: faster recovery requires more frequent backups and tested restore procedures. Regularly review logs and replace drives showing early SMART warnings rather than waiting for failure.

keyIdea.text: Combine SMART monitoring, scheduled checks, and tested backups to reduce incidents and shorten recovery time.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Monitoring & Prevention
SMART checks
sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda
# Important attributes: Reallocated_Sector_Ct, Current_Pending_Sector
Schedule smartctl or smartd checks and alert on rising reallocated or pending counts. Early replacement is cheaper than data recovery.
Backup & test
  • Automate regular backups and store offsite or on different hardware.
  • Perform periodic restores to validate backups are usable.
  • Document RAID rebuild and LVM restore procedures and test them in a lab.
Key Takeaway

Monitoring plus tested backups reduces downtime and prevents desperate, high-risk repairs during incidents.

screens.title: Incident checklist and recovery priorities
screens.narratorSegment: When an incident occurs, follow a disciplined checklist to avoid worsening the situation. First, document symptoms and capture logs: dmesg, syslog, and output from commands like lsblk and blkid. Second, take an image or snapshot where practical to preserve the current state before any repair attempt. Third, determine the failure layer: is it device-level, RAID, LVM, or filesystem? Use smartctl, /proc/mdstat, pvdisplay, vgdisplay, and lvdisplay to locate the root cause. Fourth, fix hardware issues first: replace failed drives and rebuild RAID arrays. Fifth, reactivate or repair LVM volumes only after lower layers are healthy. Sixth, run filesystem checks from a rescue environment and verify the results by mounting read-only and inspecting critical data. Throughout the process, communicate expected downtime and possible data loss to stakeholders. A common misconception is to prioritize restoring services over data preservation; in many cases taking a few minutes to image a device prevents irreversible data loss. Finish by restoring from backups if data is missing. This checklist helps you prioritize actions that preserve recoverable data while moving the system back to a stable state. Incident checklist and recovery priorities means preserve data with images and logs, repair hardware first, then rebuild logical and filesystem layers in order.. In practical terms, a stepwise plan to triage and recover from storage corruption. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Incident Checklist
Stepwise triage
  1. Record symptoms and collect logs (dmesg, syslog).
  2. Make a forensic image or snapshot if feasible.
  3. Identify layer: device, RAID, LVM, or filesystem.
  4. Replace failed hardware and rebuild RAID first.
  5. Reactivate LVM and repair filesystems from rescue mode.
  6. Verify integrity and restore from backup if needed.
Communication

Report the expected impact and recovery plan. Conserving recoverable data should take precedence over a rushed restore attempt.

Key Takeaway

Follow a documented checklist that preserves data first, repairs hardware second, and restores services last.

Fsck and filesystem-specific repair tools are powerful but must be run on unmounted filesystems or from rescue environments. LVM adds flexibility but requires diagnosis from physical volumes upward; fix physical disks first. RAID provides redundancy but is not a substitute for backups; rebuild carefully and monitor for multiple failures. fullNarratorScript:
Filesystems and storage layers are where your critical data lives, and corruption at any level can cause data loss or an unbootable system. In this lesson you will learn to spot early symptoms such as disappearing files, input/output errors, slow reads, or inaccessible directories, and to connect those symptoms to causes like sudden power loss, hardware defects, or improper unmounts. You will also learn the safe use of fsck and filesystem-specific tools, how to diagnose LVM and RAID failures, and when bad blocks mean a drive must be retired. Practical recovery steps include using a rescue environment to run checks, interpreting tool output, and understanding when to rebuild RAID or replace disks. Finally, we cover proactive measures: S. M. A. R. T. monitoring, regular filesystem checks, and comprehensive backups. By the end you will be able to triage a storage incident, run targeted repairs without worsening corruption, and design monitoring that reduces the chance of catastrophic data loss. Think of this chapter as both a diagnostic toolkit and a set of safe habits that protect system availability and your data.

By the end of this chapter you will identify the common symptoms and root causes of filesystem corruption, and explain why early detection matters. You will be able to run fsck and filesystem-specific tools safely, including when to use a rescue environment for root repairs, and how flags like -y and -f change behavior. You will diagnose LVM and RAID problems with the appropriate inspection commands and know the rebuild steps for degraded arrays. You will also recognize bad block patterns and use badblocks or fsck integration to mark failing sectors, and you will interpret SMART output to predict drive failure. Finally, you will design a basic prevention plan that includes monitoring, scheduled checks, and a reliable backup strategy so that you can recover from failures without catastrophic data loss. Each objective focuses on practical commands and safety, so you can act confidently when systems show signs of corruption.

These applied objectives focus on decision-making during an incident. You will practice selecting the correct filesystem checker and knowing when to prefer xfs_repair over fsck. You will interpret mdadm output to decide when to replace a failed drive and trigger a rebuild safely. You will use pvdisplay and lvdisplay to map logical volumes back to physical devices and understand when a missing PV requires drive replacement or metadata repair. For bad blocks you will run non-destructive scans and integrate findings into filesystem metadata so the OS avoids bad sectors. You will also set up a monitoring check with smartctl to capture S. M. A. R. T. attributes that indicate deteriorating drives. Each objective is paired with a small validation step so you can confirm competency in a lab: a simulated corruption on a test partition, followed by safe repair and verification. These steps emphasize safety and verification to avoid compounding data damage.

Filesystem corruption shows itself in a handful of consistent ways. Typical symptoms include Input/output error messages when reading or writing files, directories that become inaccessible, files that appear to vanish, and unusually slow file operations. These symptoms arise from either metadata damage, which affects directory structures and inodes, or data corruption where file contents are unreadable. Common causes map predictably to these symptoms: sudden power loss or incomplete writes can leave metadata inconsistent; hardware faults like bad sectors cause input and output errors and unreadable files; improper unmounts or kernel panics can leave a filesystem marked dirty; and filesystem-specific bugs or driver issues can corrupt metadata. Modern journaling filesystems mitigate some risks because they record pending metadata operations in a journal, enabling recovery of structural consistency after a crash, but they do not protect file contents from underlying disk errors. A common misconception is that running fsck will always restore lost files; fsck repairs structural consistency and may discard irrecoverably corrupted data. The practical test is to reproduce symptoms on a disposable VM, capture dmesg and syslog messages, and then correlate input and output errors with failing S. M. A. R. T. attributes to decide whether to repair or replace hardware. When you see these signs, prioritize a read-only snapshot or image, then proceed with diagnosis to avoid further damage. How confident are you at distinguishing metadata failure from raw device failure?

The fsck family is the primary utility for checking and repairing Linux filesystems. The most important safety rule is simple: only run fsck on an unmounted filesystem. Running fsck on a mounted or in-use filesystem risks further corruption because the on-disk state can change concurrently. For non-root partitions unmount them first with the umount command. For root or busy systems boot a rescue environment or single-user mode so the root filesystem can be unmounted or mounted read-only. Fsck is a front-end that dispatches to filesystem-specific checkers like fsck. ext4 or xfs_repair for XFS. Important flags change behavior: -y automatically answers yes to repair prompts, useful in controlled labs but risky in production because it accepts destructive fixes; -f forces a check even if the filesystem appears clean. For XFS, use xfs_repair and prefer a dry run with -n to preview changes without writing. A common misconception is that -y is always safe; in fact it can permit large deletions without inspection. Before running repairs, capture a disk image or snapshot if the data is valuable. After repairs, check filesystem integrity by mounting read-only and verifying key files. This process reduces guesswork and prevents accidental data loss by enforcing a disciplined, recoverable workflow.

When the root filesystem itself is corrupted, the only safe path is to isolate it from normal operations before making repairs. The typical workflow is: boot into a rescue image or live USB, or use single-user mode where possible. In a rescue environment the root filesystem is not mounted as the system root, so you can run fsck safely on the device. Begin by identifying the correct device name using lsblk and blkid to avoid operating on the wrong partition. Capture a disk image snapshot if the data is important. Then run fsck with the appropriate options; for an Ext4 root partition you might use fsck -fcc to include a bad block scan. If you must force checks, use -f judiciously. After fsck completes, mount the partition read-only and inspect critical files like /etc/fstab and boot files before rebooting. A misconception is that rebooting immediately after fsck always fixes boot issues; sometimes filesystem metadata was repaired but bootloader or kernel image files are damaged and need separate restoration. The rescue workflow both secures the data and gives you time to confirm the system boots cleanly before returning to production.

LVM adds a flexible layer between filesystems and physical disks but also adds diagnostic complexity. When a logical volume becomes inaccessible, you must examine Physical Volumes (PVs), Volume Groups (VGs), and Logical Volumes (LVs) to find where the fault lies. Start with sudo pvdisplay to list physical devices and their status, then vgdisplay to inspect the volume group and see which PVs are missing or failed, and finally lvdisplay to check the logical volumes. A typical failure path is a PV that went offline due to a bad disk or controller issue. If a PV is missing, the VG may show reduced capacity and LVs may be inactive. In software RAID setups the underlying PVs might themselves be RAID devices; check /proc/mdstat and mdadm --detail /dev/mdX to map those relationships. Replace a failed physical disk in RAID first, then allow mdadm and the RAID to rebuild before attempting LVM repairs. A frequent misconception is to try to repair LVM metadata before ensuring the underlying disks are healthy; doing so can corrupt higher-level structures. Always resolve hardware-level faults first, then rescan PVs and restore VG/LV state. The goal is to preserve logical volume metadata while restoring the missing physical pieces beneath it.

RAID provides redundancy but recovery steps depend on the RAID level and the nature of the failure. Software RAID1 and RAID5 tolerate a single disk failure (RAID1 mirrors, RAID5 stripes with parity); however, if failures exceed the array's tolerance or if metadata is corrupted, the array can degrade or fail. Start diagnosis with cat /proc/mdstat to see array state and use mdadm --detail /dev/mdX for member status. If a disk fails in RAID1 or RAID5, you can replace it and run mdadm --add to start rebuilding. Rebuilds read data from remaining members and reconstruct lost content using parity; they should be monitored closely because a second failure during rebuild can be catastrophic. Controller or metadata issues may require assembling the array manually with mdadm --assemble --force, but forcing assembly is risky and should be done only when you have a recent backup or a forensic image. A common mistake is adding a disk with an unexpected partition table; ensure new drives are prepared correctly before adding them. Monitoring arrays regularly and testing rebuilds in a lab helps you practice the exact sequence. The practical rule is: repair the lowest level first (replace physical drives), then rebuild RAID, then restore LVM or filesystem layers above it.

Bad blocks are physical defects on a storage device that make data unreadable or unwritable from those sectors. Drives often remap bad sectors internally using spare blocks, which is transparent until remapped counts climb. A small isolated bad block may be harmless once marked, but a growing number indicates imminent failure. Use badblocks to perform a scan and detect problematic sectors. For Ext-family filesystems e2fsck -c (or fsck -c) integrates badblocks results and writes those blocks into the filesystem's bad block inode so the OS will avoid allocating them. Importantly, badblocks can be run in read-only or non-destructive modes; destructive writes will overwrite data, so always use a non-destructive scan when scanning an active filesystem. If badblocks reports many errors, the correct action is to replace the drive rather than attempt elaborate repairs. A misconception is that marking bad blocks makes a failing drive healthy; marking avoids immediate allocation but does not stop the hardware from developing further defects. The practical approach is to combine badblock scans with SMART monitoring; rising reallocated or pending sector counts plus badblocks failures should trigger replacement and restore from backups.

When you suspect physical sector issues, combine badblocks and fsck to both detect and record bad sectors so the filesystem avoids them. Start with a non-destructive badblocks scan: badblocks -sv /dev/sdX shows progress and reports sector addresses. For an Ext-family filesystem, use e2fsck -c to run badblocks and then add the detected blocks to the filesystem's bad block inode. The combined command sequence safely marks bad sectors without overwriting user data. After running e2fsck -c, check the count of marked bad blocks and cross-reference with SMART attributes such as Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector to decide whether to keep or replace the drive. A common misconception is that e2fsck -c fixes all problems; marking blocks only prevents allocation to those sectors, but it cannot recover data already lost to hardware defects. After marking, monitor the drive closely and plan a replacement if new bad blocks appear. In production, perform this work during maintenance windows and always have backups.
